tone_statements.translation: Chapter 4 analyses the tone values of Hailu Hakka in Taiwan, the Chao-Hui area of China and West Borneo through Prof. Hirayama Hisao's 'tone-value circulation theory'; besides exploring the origin of the internal tone-value differences of Hailu Hakka, it also, through comparison with the Longhua subgroup of Hakka, reconstructs the possible source of the seven-tone pattern of present-day Hailu Hakka. ...the main features distinguishing the Hailu Hakka sound system from other Hakka dialects are summarised and ranked by priority as follows: ... 1. The basic or substituted value of the yinping tone is 53 (absolutely required). 2. The basic or substituted value of the yinqu tone is low falling or low level 31/21/11 (absolutely required). 3. The yangru tone's contour is slightly falling. 4. Yinqu and yangqu are not merged. ... 7. The yinru tone's contour is slightly rising.

tone_statements.translation: This study acoustically analyses the six citation tones of Miaoli Sixian Hakka ... Judging from the tone pattern chart in Fig. 1, Yinping is a tone that first falls then rises, but since the falling part lies wholly within band [3] and most of the rising part is also in band [3], with only the last 3 points really entering band [4], it is a mid rising tone [34]. ... Yangping and Shangsheng are both falling tones, their values written [31] and [42] respectively. ... Qusheng is a level tone; although its very onset falls slightly, apart from the 1st point all sampling points fall within band [4], so Qusheng is written [44]. tone_statements.quote: The number of sounds or words is increased greatly by the fact that they are pronounced in different tones, clearly distinguishing one from the other. Thus, their meanings are thoroughly distinct from one another, according to the tone in which they are pronounced. All words occur in four different tones, apart from those ending with t k p which have only two. 1. šong4 phin2 上平 High level (with a tendency to rise, particularly before lower tones such as ha4 phin2, šong4 šang1 and ha4 nyip5) [...] 2. ha4 phin2 下平 Low level (also with a tendency to rise before šong4 šang1 and ha4 nyip5) [...] 3. šong4 šang1 上聲 Low falling tone [...] 4. khi4 šang1 去聲 High falling [...] 5. šong4 nyip5 上入 High checked tone [...] 6. ha4 nyip5 下入 Low checked tone [...] The šong4 phin2 上平 and ha4 phin2 下平 usually lie about a fifth apart, thus are more or less like G and C. The khi4 šang1 去聲 and šong4 nyip5 上入 are very high and the khi4 šang1 去聲 only moves down to a medium low, but certainly not too low! In contrast to this, the šong4 šang1 上聲 and the ha4 nyip5 下入 are characteristically both very low, while the šong4 šang1 上聲 may not be commenced too high.

All words occur in four different tones, apart from those ending with t k p which have only two. 1. šong4 phin2 上平 High level (with a tendency to rise, particularly before lower tones such as ha4 phin2, šong4 šang1 and ha4 nyip5) [...] 2. ha4 phin2 下平 Low level (also with a tendency to rise before šong4 šang1 and ha4 nyip5) [...] 3. šong4 šang1 上聲 Low falling tone [...] 4. khi4 šang1 去聲 High falling [...] 5. šong4 nyip5 上入 High checked tone [...] 6. ha4 nyip5 下入 Low checked tone [...] The šong4 phin2 上平 and ha4 phin2 下平 usually lie about a fifth apart, thus are more or less like G and C. The khi4 šang1 去聲 and šong4 nyip5 上入 are very high and the khi4 šang1 去聲 only moves down to a medium low, but certainly not too low! In contrast to this, the šong4 šang1 上聲 and the ha4 nyip5 下入 are characteristically both very low, while the šong4 šang1 上聲 may not be commenced too high.

sources.quote: Regarding the lexical tones of Hailu Hakka, there are seven distinct tones (Huang and Yu, 2022). Among these, four tones are similar to the lexical tones of Mandarin (Figure 1B): the high-level tone (55-tone), which corresponds to Mandarin's Tone 1; the high rising contour tone (35-tone), which resembles Mandarin's Tone 2; the low falling tone (21-tone), akin to the half-Tone 3 in Mandarin; and the high falling tone (52-tone), which parallels Mandarin's Tone 4. tone.translation: Chapter 4 analyses the tone values of Hailu Hakka in Taiwan, the Chao-Hui area of China and West Borneo through Prof. Hirayama Hisao's 'tone-value circulation theory'; besides exploring the origin of the internal tone-value differences of Hailu Hakka, it also, through comparison with the Longhua subgroup of Hakka, reconstructs the possible source of the seven-tone pattern of present-day Hailu Hakka. ...the main features distinguishing the Hailu Hakka sound system from other Hakka dialects are summarised and ranked by priority as follows: ... 1. sources.quote: In sum, the six tones in Dongshi Hakka are represented in the present study as yinping 33, yangping 11, yinshang 31, yinqu 53, yinru 32, and yangru 54. They can be illustrated by examples from M. Chiang (1998) in (1). Notice that ru tones are realized only in stop-closed syllables while the non-ru tones occur in nasal-closed or open syllables. [...] By considering yinru and yangru to be the phonetic variants of yinshang and yinqu, respectively, Dongshi Hakka has only four lexical tones left: yinping 33, yangping 11, yinshang 31, and yinqu 53.
sources.note: Lexical tone confirmed (six surface tone categories, argued to four underlying lexical tones with ru tones as stop-syllable variants). Disyllabic sandhi is right-prominent: 'it is always the tone on the left that undergoes tone sandhi and the tone on the right that preserves its underlying tone.. Dongshi Hakka, like Mandarin, Southern Min, Tianjin, and Sixian Hakka, is a right prominent language. The stability of the tone on the right edge suggests that Dongshi Hakka is right-headed.' (p. 323). Footnote 8 (p. 323) adds that under emphasis the right syllable of a disyllabic word is lengthened
